extracted.intended_audience: scholars, students, and writers interested in the philosophy and theory of humor/comedy
extracted.subtask_description: Apply Bergson's theory to identify and evaluate comic elements: look for mechanical rigidity within the living, the human/social conditions for laughter, and which 'form' of the comic is present. Useful for literary/performative analysis or crafting comic material consistent with Bergson's framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical encrusted on the living (core theory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter arises from the contrast between mechanical rigidity and living, adaptive humanity: a 'certain mechanical inelasticity, just where one would expect to find the wide-awake adaptability and the living pliableness of a human being.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify moments where behaviour or form appears automatized or machine-like when applied to a person or living thing. Emphasize the contrast between expected adaptive responsiveness and observed mechanical inelasticity. This is Bergson's central diagnostic for the comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigidity, not ugliness (source of the comic)
rubrics_metrics.description: The laughable element is not primarily ugliness but rigidity — behaviour or form that is inelastic, fixed, or mechanical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating comedic effect, distinguish between mere physical unattractiveness (which is not itself comic for Bergson) and inflexibility/rigidity in conduct or form. Examples: a stiff posture, automatic phrase, or an inflexible routine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatic, repetitive, or mechanical behaviour applied to the living
rubrics_metrics.description: Behaviour that is automatic, repetitive or mechanical when exhibited by a living being is comic — e.g., absentmindedness, obsession, hoaxed simpleton, a man who slips because of rigid momentum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for repetition, automatisms, stereotyped responses, or rigid habits in characters or performers. Use concrete examples (slips, ritualized gestures, verbal automatisms) to justify the comic reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition — The Comic is Human
rubrics_metrics.description: We laugh only at human (or human-like) things; the comic must be applied to a living/human subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude purely inanimate oddities unless they are presented with human-like automatism. For analysis, show how the target exhibits human qualities or expectations that make its rigidity intelligible as comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition — Insensibility (audience detachment)
rubrics_metrics.description: To laugh, the audience must momentarily anesthetize sympathy: 'The greatest enemy of laughter is emotion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the audience's emotional engagement is sufficiently suspended to permit laughter. If pity, horror, or strong sympathy dominates, Bergson argues laughter will be suppressed; good comic effect often requires a degree of emotional distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition — The Social (laughter requires a group)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter is essentially a social gesture; it requires a group context and functions between people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the social setting: is laughter shared or communal? Determine how group dynamics enable, amplify, or punish comic displays. Private recognition without social transmission may not produce the same comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social function — corrective mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter acts as a social corrective: by the fear of being laughed at, society restrains eccentricity and 'softens down whatever the social body may retain of mechanical inelasticity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing comic content, examine what social norm or rigidity the laughter targets and how the laughter enforces conformity or discourages mechanical behaviour. Consider implications for satire, ridicule, and social regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form — Comic of forms (physical)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic generated by physical form — e.g., puppet-like figures, jack-in-the-box, snowball; physical shape or arrangement that suggests mechanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify visual or bodily configurations that read as mechanical rather than organic. Use stagecraft, costume, or description that emphasizes rigidity to justify this form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form — Comic of movements (gesture)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic arising from mechanical gestures or repetitive movements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on choreography, timing, and repetition. Repetition, abruptness, or stereotyped motion that negates adaptive responsiveness supports comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form — Comic of situations
rubrics_metrics.description: Situational comedy produced by runaway events, repetition, inversion, or reciprocal interference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze plot mechanics: escalation, inversion of expectation, and reciprocal obstruction often reveal mechanical patterns imposed on agents, producing laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form — Comic of words
rubrics_metrics.description: Linguistic comic: puns, automatisms of language, transposition and other verbal mechanisms that render speech mechanical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine slips of the tongue, formulaic phrases, puns, and verbal clichés that make language seem automatic. Show how verbal automatism undermines the living quality of speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form — Comic of character
rubrics_metrics.description: Character-based comic where vice or professional rigidity appears as automatism — a person becomes a caricature through fixed habits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a character's defining traits are portrayed as mechanical, stereotyped, or inflexible. Use biographies, routines, or occupational clichés as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rubric item 1 — Is there mechanical, rigid, or automatic behavior?
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct evaluative question from Bergson's compact rubric: detect mechanical or automatic behaviour in the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point to concrete actions, repeated patterns, or phrasing that shows automatism. The presence of such behaviour is the primary indicator of comic potential in Bergson's scheme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rubric item 2 — Is it applied to a living/human subject?
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the mechanical behaviour affect a living being? Laughter targets human or human-like subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate the human stakes or expectations involved — how the mechanical element violates living adaptiveness. Clarify any anthropomorphism if the target is non-human.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rubric item 3 — Is the audience emotionally detached enough to laugh?
rubrics_metrics.description: Would the audience momentarily suspend sympathy so that laughter, rather than pity or anger, is the response?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate emotional valence and context: scenes invoking pity or strong feeling may preclude laughter. Note framing devices that promote detachment (irony, distance, stylization).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rubric item 4 — Is the absurdity rooted in inflexibility (not malice)?
rubrics_metrics.description: Check that the absurdity stems from inelasticity or automatism rather than cruelty, malice, or deliberate harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate benign rigidity from situations where meanness or moral evil would make laughter inappropriate; Bergson's comic presumes harmless inflexibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rubric item 5 — Does it correct a social rigidity?
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the laughter function to point out and correct some social inelasticity, thereby serving a regulating role?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue how the comic instance highlights a social defect or stiff habit and how ridicule or laughter pressures conformity or behavioral change.
